newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Wereldhave to buy Nedlloyd property.
newsitem.headline: Wereldhave to buy Nedlloyd property.

text.p: Property fund Wereldhave NV said on Tuesday it expects to reach agreement this week to buy 11 distribution centres from transport group Nedlloyd with a total value of more than 100 million guilders.

The centres, which are located throughout the Netherlands, offer attractive returns on investment of some 10 to 11 percent and have the additional advantage that the sites have substantial adjacent lands, Wereldhave chairman Gijs Verweij told a news conference.
The centres will be rented back by various Nedlloyd units on long-term contracts with an average duration of 10 years.
After that period, Wereldhave will have the option to redevelop the sites and will own plots in areas where land is already scarce, Verweij said.

Earlier on Tuesday, Wereldhave announced its 1996 net profit or direct investment result had risen by 7.2 percent to 121.5 million guilders, 7.55 guilders per share, in line with a forecast issued in January.
The company expects earnings per share to show a further growth to 7.75 guilders in 1997 and Verweij said he expects the property markets in various countries to recover further.
Wereldhave's interest charges fell by 6.6 million guilders to 50.4 million last year and the company expects interest rates to remain low in 1997.
Operational costs are expected to show another fall in the current year after they fell by 0.9 million guilders to 13.8 million guilders in 1996. Rental income is expected to grow.
Verweij said Wereldhave will invest in various European countries this year but not, like some other real estate investors, in the Far East and not in Germany or Spain.
Issues of new shares to finance investments are unlikely, as the company has ample liquid assets, he said.
These liquid funds were boosted by the sale of the Carnaby Estate property in London to Shaftesbury Plc which was finalised earlier this month.

Verweij said the Carnaby deal had brought in a "substantial" book profit which had exceeded both Wereldhave's estimates and those of other parties included. Shaftesbury said in November it would pay 90 million stg for the shopping properties.

For the first time in years, Wereldhave could positively revalue its property in 1996 and its value rose by 1.5 percent to 2.51 billion guilders. But Verweij said it was too early to say this might be the start of a longer-term revaluation trend.
Wereldhave intends to pay an unchanged 1996 dividend of 7.25 guilders per share but shareholders can also opt for a payment in new shares, the details of which will be given on March 14.
Investors have the choice of a full dividend payment in shares this year, which is tax-friendly for private Dutch investors.

Verweij said shareholders will also have the option to take up a large part of their dividend in shares next year but the optional stock dividend payment might fall in subsequent years as the company is forced to pay out more of its net profits.
